newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada bonds close stronger, disregard weak dollar.
newsitem.headline: Canada bonds close stronger, disregard weak dollar.

text.p: Canadian bonds closed much stronger on Friday as traders disregarded weakness in the currency and focused on recent comments from U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, analysts said.

"Underlying everything is the notion that Greenspan has delivered a heavy hint in the mind of the market that he's not going to be raising rates in May," said Jim Webber, director of fixed-income research with TD Securities Inc.
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$0.80 to C$110.75 to yield 7.089 percent.
The U.S. 30-year bond rose 16/32 to yield 6.89 percent. The spread between the two bonds narrowed to 20 basis points from 23 basis points at Thursday's close.

Greenspan said in a speech on Thursday he expected economic growth to slow later this year and into next, but added that the central bank would need to act if that did not prove to be the case. The speech spurred a rally in Canadian and U.S. fixed-income markets as investors viewed it as a signal that U.S. rates would not rise on May 20.
But that view failed to support the Canadian dollar, which fell sharply against the U.S. dollar and Japanese yen.
Webber said Canada's outperformance relative to U.S. treasuries was unusual given the weak currency, but said it might be linked to Canadian employment data out this morning.
Statistics Canada on Friday said the unemployment rate rose to 9.6 percent in April from 9.3 percent in March, although the economy added 33,000 new jobs.

"What it indicated is we can create an awful lot of jobs month to month without reducing the unemployment rate. Therefore even if we do create jobs, the necessity for the Bank of Canada actually to tighten monetary conditions is maybe some way away," said Webber.
In other prices, Canada's 10-year benchmark bond rose C$0.63 to C$103.20 to yield 6.543 percent. The U.S. bond rose 15/32 to yield 6.67 percent.
The negative spread between the two bonds widened to 13 basis points from 10 basis points at the close of trading on Thursday.
The three-month cash T-bill traded with a yield of 3.05 percent against its U.S. equivalent, which yielded 5.16 percent.
